note: HL05 chapter capability ledger. Authored intent, not a derived cache: no validator may rewrite this file. Chapters 6 through 9 are authorable today. Chapters 1-5 are entirely schema-v1 (no introduces/practises knowledge atoms), so no payoff there can name atoms a lesson actually practises; they are deliberately absent rather than stubbed, and that absence is real, measurable debt.

chapters.title: Numbers One to Five
chapters.label: ch:numbers-one-to-five
chapters.canDo: I can count from one to five in headless Gujarati script and explain why બે starts with b where its neighbours start with d, and why ત્રણ has an r that Hindi tīn does not.

payoff.summary: Take the two odd numerals apart: બે descends from the feminine/neuter dvé by dv → bb → b, while ત્રણ's r is a learned restoration from Sanskrit, put back after Prakrit tiṇṇi had already dropped it.

chapters.title: Six Verbs at the Core
chapters.label: ch:gu-core-verbs
chapters.canDo: I can name six everyday Gujarati verbs by the neuter -વું ending they all share, strip that ending to reach the stem, and say what I do with stem, person-ending, and the copula છે.

payoff.summary: The sixth verb runs the whole chapter at once: strip the neuter -વું from all six infinitives, hold the retroflex ણ that Prakrit pulled back from a plain n, put the stem into hũ jāṇũ chhũ, and connect jāṇvũ to the English know it is genuinely cousin to.

chapters.title: The Mind and the Page
chapters.label: ch:gu-mind-and-page
chapters.canDo: I can say that I think, understand, read and write in Gujarati, hear and write the nasal that sits in the middle of વાંચવું, and name what each of the four roots was doing before it meant a mental act — ranging about, waking up, speaking, and scratching.

payoff.summary: Say હું મારું નામ લખું છું, run the chapter's four verbs back with the four things their roots meant — vichārvũ from a root meaning to range about, samajvũ from one meaning to wake, vā̃chvũ from one meaning to speak, lakhvũ from one meaning to scratch — place the medial nasal of vā̃ch- and the assimilate-then-simplify path from dhy to j, and say which of the four honestly has no English cousin at all.

chapters.title: Taking, Asking, Helping, Liking
chapters.label: ch:gu-doing-verbs
chapters.canDo: I can take, ask, help and say what I like in Gujarati, explain why મદદ કરવી ends in the feminine -ી while કામ કરવું ends in the neuter, and say why મને ગુજરાતી ગમે છે leaves no room for me as its subject.

payoff.summary: Say મને ગુજરાતી ગમે છે and hear that you are not its subject, set it against હું ગુજરાતી બોલું છું where you are, trace ગમવું back to gamyate — the passive of gam- 'to go', so the verb was born without a doer and is English come besides — and run the chapter's four verbs back with where each came from: Sanskrit prek- behind pūchhvũ, lebh- behind levũ, Arabic madad through Persian, and the feminine ending madad forces onto karvī.
